newsitem.title: JAPAN: Donors pledge $2.9 bln in aid to Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Donors pledge $2.9 bln in aid to Philippines.

text.p: The Philippines won aid pledges worth $2.9 billion at an annual meeting of donor nations on Wednesday, half of it from Japan, World Bank officials said.

"A total amounting to about $2.9 billion has been agreed...of which Japan will provide $1.4 billion," Javad K. Shirazi, a World Bank East Asia and Pacific Region director, told a news conference in Tokyo.

A large slice of the aid package, which consisted of $400 million in grants and $2.5 billion in loans, was earmarked for the island of Mindanao, the scene of fierce fighting in recent years between Moslem rebels and government forces.
Asked how much was needed for the development of relatively backward Mindanao, Philippines Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said the aid package was not enough.
Ocampo added: "$400 million are devoted to Mindanao, but of course these are just startups because the needs are vast..."

The Japanese government said it would fund development projects in Mindanao after Philippine President Fidel Ramos signed a peace agreement with the main Moslem rebel group, the Moro National Liberation Front, in September.

Comparing his country to fast-developing Asian nations such as South Korea and Taiwan, named the Asian Tigers, Ocampo said the Philippines was beginning to attract high-tech industries from its neighbours.

"The Philippines is a tiger cub... we're still growing. In the computer technology field a number of firms have been moving to the Philippines because of the vast pool of English-speaking, technically skilled workers," he said.
The World Bank chaired the sixth annual consultative meeting of the Philippine Assistance Programme (PAP), launched in 1989 to help restructure the Philippine economy.
Before the meeting, the Philippine government had said it expected $2.55 billion in new aid pledges.
The World Bank said donors praised the 7.1 percent growth rate in the first three quarters of this year as a result of what they said was Manila's strong economic management.

But donors called on the Philippines to strengthen the economy's resilience to external shocks, particularly in view of the rising trade and current account deficits, and the increased reliance on potentially volatile capital inflows, the World Bank said.
